title: Calgary's police chief, mayor weigh in on fatal police shooting
subtitle: 'Much has been reported about Mr. Tuel's challenges with his mental health and that he had been struggling of late. But the call that the police responded to was not - when reported - about mental health,' Neufeld said
article: Calgary Mayor Jyoti Gondek says it is a "sorrowful time in our community" after a Black man was shot and killed by police on the weekend.
The city's police chief defended his officers' actions while providing more details about the incident Tuesday. He has yet to talk to the man's family.

Latjor Tuel, 41, was fatally shot by police officers Saturday during an altercation in Forest Lawn in which he allegedly attacked a police service dog. The city's South Sudanese community and Tuel's family are grieving his death and questioning official accounts .

"We're grieving the loss of a man who had tremendous impact within his community, not only the neighbourhood he lived in but the Sudanese community in Calgary. This is a person who was loved by friends and family," said Gondek.

"I'm concerned that we haven't managed to build a strong enough network yet, for newcomers to be supported when they come here."
Gondek said work needs to be done to strengthen the city's social support and mental-health networks.

"As the Calgary Police Service continues to work with its anti-racism committee and with the diversity advisory boards, and as they continue to reach out to the community and Mr. Tuel's family, we remain committed as a city to do everything we can," said Gondek.
She urged members of the Calgary police commission to ask difficult questions at Wednesday's meeting.
Police Chief Mark Neufeld said during a news conference Tuesday he has met with members of the Sudanese community but not directly with Tuel's family.
Neufeld provided more details about the shooting in an effort to quell misinformation he said is spreading online.

"Much has been reported about Mr. Tuel's challenges with his mental health and that he had been struggling of late. But the call that the police responded to was not - when reported - about mental health. It was a complaint of an assault involving a man in possession of a knife and a stick in a busy public area," said Neufeld.

Tuel's family told reporters he was a South Sudanese refugee who came to Calgary about 20 years ago and suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder related to his time as a child soldier in his home country.
Neufeld defended police response to the incident, saying it would have been a difficult situation for mental-health workers because of the stick and knife Tuel was holding.
The police commission said the fatal shooting will be discussed at Wednesday's meeting.
"Saturday's police shooting was a tragedy not only for the loved ones of the man who died, but also for our community," the police commission said in a statement to Postmedia.

"Improving the de-escalation practices and use-of-force options available to officers remains a priority for our commission, as do looking for better ways to respond when people are in crisis and ensuring equity for all people in our city. We are committed to following this investigation closely to ensure the service is doing everything it can to prevent deaths like this in the future."

Coun. Courtney Walcott, who sits on the police commission, said he hopes the meeting can provide the public with information about what goes into de-escalation measures, what the protocols are for using canines and how the police engage with people who are in crisis.
"So we can further understand some of the tragedy that we witnessed on the weekend and, of course, to push for the necessary changes or growth in the system that may be required," said Walcott.

"I think that's really what police commission is going to be about this week, is taking a look at everything we saw and asking ourselves some pretty serious questions about whether or not this is how we want to exist in our relationship with the police service."
Coun. Gian-Carlo Carra, who also sits on police commission, said in a statement he was saddened by Tuel's killing.
"I count a huge proportion of Calgary's South Sudanese community as my Ward 9 constituents and I count many of their leaders as friends," said Carra.
He said the shooting is a condemnation of the slow pace with which the city is reforming policing and emergency response.

"We need to rectify the fact that we have no idea what a different and better end state for policing, emergency response and the continuum of care would actually look like and how it would actually function in Calgary," he said.
"I'm working with commission, city administration and my colleagues on council to put together a council innovation fund proposal to do that work."
ActionDignity, an organization that supports newcomers and racialized people in Calgary, said in a statement that the incident has made many Black and racialized people in the city feel unsafe.
"ActionDignity is putting a pause to its system change work with the Calgary police to grieve with the family and communities and reflect on our actions," the statement said.
Notices for a protest scheduled for outside city hall on Friday at 1 p.m. were floating around social media Tuesday.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) confirmed Tuesday it is investigating the shooting and will examine the circumstances surrounding the officer's use of force.

In a news release Tuesday, ASIRT said Calgary police responded to calls about a man on 17th Avenue S.E. near 44th Street who was holding a stick and knife around 3:41 p.m. Saturday. Officers arrived minutes later and surrounded the man from a distance, according to ASIRT.

ASIRT said Tuel was sitting on the sidewalk before he got up and an officer discharged less-lethal baton rounds at him. Tuel allegedly ran toward a group of officers and a police service dog on a leash was allowed to run toward the man.
"Video shows that the dog's handler pulled the dog back, upon which the man advanced in the direction of the dog and the handler," said ASIRT.
Tuel then allegedly swung the stick and stabbed the knife at the dog while the dog bit him. The dog was injured.
Officers used their conductive energy weapons - or Tasers - and ASIRT said a confrontation occurred in which two officers shot Tuel.
EMS had been waiting nearby but Tuel was pronounced dead at the scene.
ASIRT is asking witnesses or people with video of the incident to contact investigators at 403-592-4306.
